title: Study on the Helpfulness of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to evaluate the helpfulness of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods using objective, human-centered measures rather than relying only on subjective satisfaction or opinion. The authors argue that existing XAI evaluations are often context-dependent and that many user studies do not directly measure whether explanations help people perform a relevant task. To address this, they propose an objective proxy-task methodology in which explanation quality is judged by whether users can correctly infer aspects of model behavior.

The studied approach is a user study comparing six XAI methods: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and Confidence Scores. Participants viewed image, explanation, and ground-truth information and had to determine whether an AI model’s prediction was correct, whether it could be trusted, and whether it should be questioned. The underlying models were AlexNet and VGG16 applied to ImageNetV2 images. The design uses objective correctness outcomes rather than self-reported preference as the main metric.

The participants were 139 volunteers recruited through Technische Universität Berlin social media, with many undergraduates and graduate/postgraduate students; the paper also notes the sample had a strong university background. The study found that all methods performed above chance for judging correctness, but Confidence Scores performed best overall for accuracy; Grad-CAM, Confidence Scores, and LRP performed best for trust, while SHAP performed best for questioning AI decisions. The authors conclude that no single explanation method is sufficient for all goals, and recommend combining explanation methods in an interactive framework. They also note important caveats: the task is staged, depends on domain knowledge, and may not generalize cleanly to real-world use cases.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological/user-study paper about XAI evaluation, not a K-12 educational intervention study. It does not evaluate a classroom instructional treatment, target-domain science reasoning outcome, or any K-12 learner effects, so it does not meet credibility/relevance criteria for the requested evidence base.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact on K-12 science learning is reported. The findings concern adult participants’ ability to judge AI outputs in an image-classification proxy task, so there is no evidence of impact on student scientific reasoning or inquiry outcomes.

interventions.use_case: human-centered evaluation of explainable AI (XAI) methods for judging AI image-classification correctness using proxy decision tasks
